column11: NCT07746089 (book trials table: randomised, quadruple-blind, treatment; primary outcome 'Change from baseline at week 24 in 6MWT distance'); argenx release 2025-06-30 (argenx.com/news/2025/press-release-3107132) describes the Phase 3 as placebo-controlled 'with an Open-Label Extension'; a subcutaneous formulation is in a Phase 1 bioavailability study (NCT07673601, context file)
column12: CMS is a lifelong genetic disorder. A receptor agonist works only while exposure lasts, so dosing continues as maintenance, and the open-label extension and the SC formulation in development both point that way. The dosing interval is not public

column11: lookup.py demand Vyvgart: CMS Medicare Part B 2024, $416,589,120.90 over 1,803 beneficiaries = $231,053 per beneficiary. The same anchor the book's nipocalimab seed uses
column12: Judgement on the comparator. No drug is approved in CMS: argenx says there are no approved treatments for DOK7-CMS (release 2025-06-30), and amifampridine failed its Phase 3 in CMS (practicalneurology.com, 'Treatment for Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes Fails to Meet Primary Endpoint in Phase 3 Clinical Trial'). Vyvgart IV is argenx's own IV antibody for a disease of the same synapse, and neuromuscular specialists prescribe both. Both are physician-infused and billed under Part B, which fits a Part B anchor. Case for higher: CMS is ultra-rare, about 2,200 US patients against 82,715 with MG (the book's pool), and ultra-orphan neuromuscular drugs sell for more. Evrysdi, in SMA, where adimanebart is also in Phase 2, reads $328,087 per Part D beneficiary in 2024; Ultomiris reads $330,448 per Part B beneficiary; Vyvgart itself reads $254,275 per Part D beneficiary (all lookup.py demand). Case for lower: 124 of 442 UK patients are children (Rossini 2025), and weight-based dosing would use less drug per child

column11: house convention for a CMS Part B anchor (backend/gross_to_net.py): Part B pays 106% of average sales price, and ASP is already net of discounts, so only the add-on comes off: 1 - 1/1.06. The nipocalimab and pozelimab seeds use the same value on Part B anchors
column12: Direction checked: 5.66% off list, so net is $217,975 per patient-year. Part B holds because CoMetS doses adimanebart IV. Case against: if the SC formulation in Phase 1 (NCT07673601) were the commercial product, it would move to pharmacy benefit, where the house 0.5 applies. The population is also young (median age 29 in the UK cohort), so Medicaid and commercial rebates, which sit outside ASP, would weigh more than in gMG

column12: Judgement: no persistence data exist for any CMS therapy, since none is approved. The book's gMG figure counts only stops for non-response and adverse events, the reasons that would apply in a genetic disease with no remission. Case for lower: CMS does not remit and has no approved alternative, so a responder has no reason to stop. The pozelimab second read bracketed gMG persistence down to 0.142. Case for higher: IV infusion burden in children, and the book's nipocalimab seed uses 0.5 for real-world anti-FcRn persistence. That gMG figure includes stopping in remission, which CMS lacks

column12: Judgement on the review timeline. Readout around the end of 2030 and a BLA in 2031. As the first therapy for a serious disease with none approved, a priority review is plausible; it follows from a significant improvement in a serious condition, not from orphan status, and runs about eight months from submission for an original BLA. That puts approval around the turn of 2032, and 2032 is taken as the first full year. This is the same PCD-to-first-full-year gap the vepugratinib seed uses (PCD 2029-10 to 2031). Not announced by argenx. Case for later: a standard twelve-month review of a mid-2031 filing puts approval in mid-2032 and the first full year in 2033, and a 105-patient trial across four genotypes, not yet recruiting at its last update (2026-08-04), may enrol slowly

Royalty paid, netted as (0.2335 - 0.01) / 0.2335 = 0.9572
column12: JUDGEMENT on the tier: 'low single digits' is taken at its bottom, 1%, as the litifilimab seed takes 'mid-single-digit' at 4% and the disitamab vedotin seed takes 'high single digit' at 7%. The engine applies economics_share to the rNPV, and the build's costs scale with revenue, so a royalty on sales takes its share of the margin. Milestones are not netted, as in the other royalty seeds. Case against: 3%, the top of 'low single digits', gives 0.8715, and 2% gives 0.9143. The rate is tiered, and the filing words one royalty for two licensors, NYU Langone and LUMC, so the combined rate could sit above the floor. The FY2025 20-F drops the licence section but still calls the NYU Langone and LUMC patent families in-licensed; unlike Broteio for empasiprubart, the licensors are universities argenx has not acquired, so the royalty is taken to run. There is no co-commercialisation partner. A Halozyme ENHANZE royalty would apply only to a subcutaneous product (SC formulations are in Phase 1, NCT07673601); CoMetS doses IV

column11: Rossini E et al., 'Prevalence and Geographical Distribution of Patients With Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes in the United Kingdom', Muscle Nerve 2025, PMID 41251564, PMC12690014, doi:10.1002/mus.70063. There were 442 living, genetically confirmed patients on 2023-12-31, a prevalence of 6.5 per million (95% CI 5.9-7.2). Applied to the US resident population of 341,784,857 on 2025-07-01 (Census Bureau Vintage 2025, census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-national-total.html): 6.5 x 341.78 = 2,222
column12: Judgement: a UK rate transferred to the US, since no US prevalence study was found. lookup.py pool returns nothing for this indication, so the book carries no competing figure. A genetically confirmed count fits a label that requires a genotype. Case for higher: the same study finds 8.8 per million in regions with a specialised neuromuscular service against 5.9 elsewhere, and reads that as underdiagnosis. Case for lower: argenx puts CMS at about 5 per million (release 2025-06-30, via search, page not opened), Turkey measures 4.49 (PMID 41059415), Belgium 3.19 (PMID 38964204) and Austria 3.1. Prevalence and incidence differ here, so the engine keeps its default carryover of 1.0. That is right for a lifelong genetic disease: an untreated patient stays eligible. US test (second reader): no US prevalence study exists. The one US count found is a claims study on Komodo Health Prism, 2018 to September 2022 (ISPOR 2026 poster, 'Real-world demographic and treatment characteristics of patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome in the United States', via search, page not opened): 336 patients with at least two G70.2 claims 30 or more days apart or one inpatient claim, after excluding anyone with two or more claims for myasthenia gravis, LEMS or a muscular dystrophy, out of about 300 million covered lives. That is about 1.1 per million, or 383 on the Census population, a sixth of 2,222. It is a floor, not a prevalence: the exclusion removes CMS patients also coded as MG, the commonest misdiagnosis; claims capture of an ultra-rare disease over a short window is incomplete; and the cohort is 63% under 18 against 28% (124 of 442) in the UK genetic cohort, which points to adults missing from US claims. It is still the case for lower that bears most directly on the US: the pool a US payer can identify today is far smaller than a UK diagnostic rate implies, and 2,222 assumes US genetic diagnosis reaches the UK rate by launch

column11: Inan et al., 'Epidemiological study of congenital myasthenic syndromes based on national electronic health database of Turkiye', North Clin Istanb 2025, PMID 41059415, PMC12497907, doi:10.14744/nci.2025.08455: '0.63' new cases per million in 2023 (406 patients with at least three ICD-10 G70.2 entries, 2015-2024). 0.63 x 341.78 = 215 US a year
column12: Judgement: the only national CMS incidence figure found, applied to the US population. It counts new coded diagnoses, which is the inflow to a diagnosed pool, rather than births. Case for lower: the same registry reports 0.28 to 0.59 per million over 2016 to 2023, so 2023 is the high point. The diagnoses are coded, not genetically confirmed. Turkey's consanguinity raises recessive disease rates. Case for higher: UK underdiagnosis (above) and argenx's natural-history study (NCT06078553) and awareness work may speed genetic diagnosis once a therapy exists. The engine filters it by eligible_pct, about 41 US DOK7 diagnoses a year. US test (second reader): the one US population-based figure is Olmsted County, Minnesota (Mansukhani SA et al., Am J Ophthalmol 2019, PMID 30653958, doi:10.1016/j.ajo.2019.01.004): CMS incidence 0.23 per 100,000 under 19 a year (95% CI 0.005 to 0.46), from 4 cases over 1966 to 2015, 3 of them siblings, in a county whose care is almost all at Mayo Clinic, a CMS referral centre. On the 73,132,720 US residents under 18 (Census Vintage 2024: 340,110,988 less 266,978,268 adults, the figures the book uses) that is about 168 childhood diagnoses a year, above the 126 the Turkish rate implies for childhood (0.63 x 58.6% diagnosed before 18 x 341.78). So the US figure does not argue for lower, but its interval runs from about 4 to 336 a year. Against: the US claims count of 336 coded patients over 2018 to September 2022 (ISPOR 2026 poster, see prevalence) is hard to square with 215 new coded diagnoses a year

column11: Rossini et al., Muscle Nerve 2025 (PMID 41251564, PMC12690014), the same cohort as the prevalence: of 442 UK patients, mutations in the AChR/CHRNE group, DOK7 and RAPSN were most common, at 37%, 19% and 16%. The full-text sentence italicises the gene names; the abstract names 'CHRNE deficiency, DOK7, RAPSN' in that order. Cross-checks: DOK7 was 44 of 235 (18.7%) in the French adult cohort (Theuriet et al., Brain 2024, PMID 38696726, doi:10.1093/brain/awae124). UK 6.5 x 0.19 = 1.24 DOK7 patients per million, against argenx's 1.2 per million (release 2025-06-30, via search)
column12: Judgement, and a floor on the label. The label population is CoMetS's four genotypes. DOK7 is the only one the UK text quantifies. MUSK, AGRN and LRP4 are left out: Engel et al. (Lancet Neurol 2015, PMID 25792100, PMC4520251) count six reports of MUSK-CMS, three of agrin deficiency and one LRP4 patient. The French cohort's heat map, which by its methods includes only genotypes with at least four patients, carries MUSK and AGRN, so each is at least 1.7% of French adults. Case for higher: adding those two gives about 0.22, and argenx's own figure for DOK7 is about 24% of CMS (release 2025-06-30, via search). Case for lower: a 6MWT primary endpoint implies ambulatory patients. If the label or payers follow the entry criteria, non-ambulatory and ventilated patients may be excluded; at last visit 36.3% of French DOK7 adults used a wheelchair (Theuriet 2024). The age floor of CoMetS could not be read, since ClinicalTrials.gov is blocked here and the Amass quota is exhausted

Scaling to Vyvgart's stock share at this discontinuation would give 0.2156 x 0.2704/0.5 = 0.1166, the case for lower. Other points for lower: a genotype is needed first, IV infusions for children, and DOK7 patients already respond to off-label salbutamol or ephedrine (Engel 2015). Case for higher: this would be the first and only approved CMS therapy, in a small, concentrated, specialist-managed population already identified through argenx's natural-history study. On these inputs about 235 US patients are on therapy at the 2040 plateau, 56% of the 422 US eligible
